title: You Said: The Fugitive Light of Your Hair...
text:
You said: the fugitive light of your hair

had taken refuge on the pillow

and when I brought my hands near

they turned to water for me,

silk of water.

I felt my body a sea and you upon the beach.

You said: do not spread any more

the musical waterfall,

I want you like this, dressed

in silence and in nothing.

I want you like this, silky,

like this, helpless.

You said it. Because you loved me.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the intimate second-person address and the hair/water/sea imagery of Soler's love poem.

title: I Feel Sorry for the One Who Wanted...
text:
I feel sorry for the one who wanted

to reach an ideal,

struggled and did not arrive.

But I feel sorrier

for the one who did not try to arrive

because he thought

it was not worth the trouble.

And stayed where he was.

I feel sorry

for the one who wanted to dream

and believed in his own dreams

until he woke up.

But sorrier

for the one who never had dreams

and died without having dreamed.

I feel sorry for the flower

and sorrier for the stone

that never flowered.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the plain moral contrast between failed striving and never daring to dream.

title: Smuggling and Misery...
text:
Smuggling and misery.

Shacks, prostitutes,

sweat and clouds of dust.

Children with sad eyes

and swollen bellies.

Calvary of women border-porters.

Frontier.

Hunger, dirty deals.

Rachitic soldiers

and fat generals.


Sergeants, foremen

of whip and cane,

cards and shootouts.

Frontier.

There the land wounded

on all four sides.

The people raw flesh.

Smuggling and misery.

The whole homeland a frontier!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the clipped indictment of the border as exploitation, hunger, and a wounded homeland.

title: Captive Blood
text:
Indian blood, Indian blood is in my people.

It burns!

In the wounded quebracho of my forests.

It suffers!

In the green hell of the miner.

It moans!

In the mouth of stifled complaints.

It boils!

It has bitten the entrails of my land.

It rises!

Slowly chewing its chains.

It roars!

Driving the life that dawns.

It cries out!

Its sacred right to be blood.

Free!

Indian blood, Indian blood is in my people.

It fights!
editorial_note: The translation preserves Soler's chant-like sequence of blood as captive, Indigenous, and revolutionary force.

title: Canoe
text:
Canoe upriver,

canoe downriver.

The rich man lives off the poor

and the poor man off his work.


The fisherman fishes

what he cannot

and keeps checking

the longlines.


Canoe upriver,

canoe downriver,

he starves

with his work.


The fisherman fishes

what he does not want:

his misery of children

dying on him.


Canoe upriver,

canoe downriver.

The rich man lives off the poor

and the poor man off his work.


And here a period must be put:

the woman suffers it

for all of them together.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the river-song refrain and the economic critique of fishing labor and family suffering.
